source: Clement & Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping (Exp 1, importance judgments)
finding: People judging which matched facts belong to an analogy preferred the fact embedded in a shared causal system over an equally matching isolated fact.
numbers: Exp 1: 48 paid Illinois undergraduates (24 analogy, 24 target-only control). Analogy group chose the shared-system fact 67% to 92% of the time across 4 passages; target-only controls chose it 42% to 54%. Group difference significant (Fisher exact, p<.05) in 3 of 4 passages.
limits: Short invented science passages, read and memorised. The control group matters: it rules out that the shared-system fact was simply more salient. Only 3 of 4 passages showed the effect.
agent_relevance: Systematicity is a real selection constraint, but shown with small samples and contrived stories. A code-scored systematicity needs the same control: compare against the same case without the base.

source: Clement & Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping (Exp 2, predictions)
finding: When asked to predict a new fact about the target, analogy subjects predicted the fact that linked into the matching causal system, not an equally plausible isolated fact.
numbers: Exp 2: 32 subjects (16 per group). Net shared-minus-different predictions: M=1.63 for analogy group vs M=0 for target-only; F(1,28)=20.05, p<.001. Rating task: shared-system facts M=6.03 vs different-system M=4.41. Choice task: analogy subjects picked the shared-system fact 87% and 69% on two passages vs 44% and 25% for controls; the other two passages were weaker (62% and 75% vs 69% and 44%).
limits: Small N. One passage was flagged as possibly biased and dropped in one analysis (F(1,28)=13.03 without it). Base passage was in view.
agent_relevance: Candidate inferences should come from the connected system that matches, not from loose similarity. This is the core rule O7 would implement.

source: Clement & Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping (Exp 3, from memory)
finding: With the base passage removed (recall only), the systematicity preference held overall but failed on one passage whose base was poorly remembered.
numbers: Exp 3: 46 subjects (24 analogy). Condition x fact-type interaction in ratings F(1,44)=10.82, p<.01; choice-count difference vs control (M=1), F(1,44)=13.15, p=.001. On Passage 2 the proportion choosing the shared-system fact was .54 vs .58 (no effect). On the base-comprehension test for Passage 2, 42% of subjects missed the key point (poor encoding of the base).
limits: The one failing item is explained by weak encoding of the base, not a refutation, but it shows the effect needs a well-understood base.
agent_relevance: A mapping can only be as good as the stored base. Check that the base was understood before trusting a mapping score.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat UCLA students on zero-shot text analogies: digit matrices, letter strings, four-term verbal analogies.
numbers: Digit matrices: GPT-3 above 40 humans, OR=1.88, p=.005. Letter strings: GPT-3 above 57 humans overall, OR=1.76, p=6.3e-5, driven by zero-generalization problems. Pattern of difficulty correlated with humans on matrices, r(30)=0.39. Above the estimated average high-school SAT-analogy level.
limits: Problems may overlap web text. Performance dropped when prompt format changed (Suppl. Fig 5). code-davinci-002 did near chance on verbal analogies.
agent_relevance: Large models do simple relational induction without a scaffold. This is a baseline: scaffold gains must be shown above it.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) story analogies (higher-order relations)
finding: Direct test of the systematicity preference with Gentner's story sets: GPT-3 chose the causally matching story only for near analogies, not far ones. GPT-4 did better.
numbers: Humans N=54: overall t(53)=21.3; near t(53)=21.5; far t(53)=16.7; 15 of 54 picked the analogous story on every trial. GPT-3 binomial: overall p=.0005, near p=.0039, far p=.065 (not significant). Humans beat GPT-3, OR=0.37, p=.0003. GPT-4 near almost perfect, far more robust but only some sensitivity to higher-order relations.
limits: GPT-4 was a preliminary check. Far analogy (different entities, shared relations) is the case that tests real structure mapping and was the weak one.
agent_relevance: The systematicity preference is weakest exactly where it matters (far analogy). Do not trust an LLM judge alone for far mappings; score with code.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: On letter-string analogies with permuted or symbol alphabets, humans stayed high while GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 all fell. Argues earlier success relied on familiar material.
numbers: Overall accuracy: humans 0.753 (1,876 samples; 136 Prolific recruits, 2 rejected), GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452 (6,840 samples each). Human accuracy flat across 0, 2, 5, 10, 20 permuted letters and symbols; GPT dropped, with a further drop for symbol alphabets. Comprehension checks near 1.0 for GPT-3.5/4, so they understood successor and predecessor.
limits: Humans here scored higher than Webb's 57 students on the baseline, so the human reference moved. Prompt format mattered; best format borrowed from Hodel and West.
agent_relevance: Format-bound analogy skill. Test O7 on mappings with relabeled symbols, not only on natural content.

source: Hodel & West (2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Failed generalisation: simple variations of the original letter-string tasks (synthetic alphabet, larger interval) broke GPT-3 while humans stayed high.
numbers: GPT-3 kept performance on only 2 of 6 problem types (remove-redundant-letter, sort) on the counterexamples; these are the two where no new letter has to be generated. Human accuracy about the same across modifications.
limits: GPT-3 only. Webb and colleagues replied that the failure may be a counting problem, not an analogy problem.
agent_relevance: Second independent failure on shifted problems. Treat a score on a familiar-format analogy test as an upper bound.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs (reply)
finding: The permuted-alphabet failure was traced to indexing letters in the shuffled list. GPT-4 with code execution matched humans.
numbers: Interval-1 humans N=99, interval-2 N=97. GPT-4 vs humans: P=8.9e-13 (humans better). GPT-4 with code execution vs humans: P=0.496 (no difference); interval-size effect not significant with code (P=0.066). 46% of GPT-4 errors used a valid alternative rule vs 39% of human errors.
limits: Authors' own reply, so not independent. Code use is not a human route. Does not rescue the far-analogy story result.
agent_relevance: Tool use fixes the part that is computation (counting, indexing). Supports a typed mapping scored by code in O7.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Millière & Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning (J. Memory and Language 145)
finding: Tasks mapping meaningful words to symbols. Best LLMs matched humans in the default condition but were more fragile to scrambled order and to irrelevant semantic structure.
numbers: Default condition: GPT-4 (p=.097), Claude 3 (p=.194), Llama-405B (p=.097) not different from humans. Permuted pairs: significant drops for Claude 3 (z=-4.2), GPT-4 (z=-4.0), Llama-405B (z=-5.5); humans unaffected. Random-structure conditions: humans fell about 0.15, Claude 3 about 0.5, GPT-4 0.6 and 0.4. Random-finals: humans down about 0.5, GPT-4 down 0.8. Dual-attribute: GPT-4 about 0.7 vs humans about 0.4.
limits: Human sample recruited by email (paid $10); performance varied strongly with prompt wording (Only-RHS condition ranged 20% to 100% across prompts).
agent_relevance: LLMs beat humans on some compositional mappings and are worse at ignoring distractors. A typed mapping with an explicit one-to-one constraint targets the weak spot.

source: Yuan et al. (2023) Beneath Surface Similarity: LLMs make reasonable scientific analogies after structure abduction (SCAR)
finding: On 400 scientific system analogies (camera to eye) needing one-to-one concept mappings, LLMs lag humans. Models do well on word analogies but poorly on the structure behind them.
numbers: SCAR: 400 analogies, 1,614 concept mappings, 13 fields. Table (layout garbled, figures approximate): GPT-4 about 73% and best config (1-shot plus background) about 77%; ChatGPT about 66% to 74%; humans (2 graduate students) about 86%. Embedding max-similarity mapping was poor; greedy and Kuhn-Munkres one-to-one assignment over embeddings were clearly better.
limits: Only two human raters. Models were sensitive to instruction wording.
agent_relevance: A one-to-one assignment algorithm over similarity scores beat free mapping. Supports letting code enforce the one-to-one constraint.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) StoryAnalogy: story-level analogies from LLMs
finding: Identifying story-level analogies was very hard for sentence embeddings and LLMs.
numbers: 24K story pairs annotated on two similarities from extended structure-mapping theory. ChatGPT about 30% on multiple choice vs over 85% for humans. Fine-tuned FlanT5-xxl matched zero-shot ChatGPT on analogy generation.
limits: Abstract and introduction only; results tables not read.
agent_relevance: Far, story-level mapping is a known weak spot; do not rely on a model's judgment of it.

source: Khojasteh et al. (2026) YARN: structural mapping with LLM-derived abstractions for narrative analogy
finding: A code mapping step over LLM-extracted event units failed without abstraction and beat LLM-only with abstraction on one benchmark.
numbers: Structural mapping without abstraction: Qwen MCQ 0.17 (random 0.25) and 0.24 on far ARN analogies (random 0.50). With abstractions: Qwen 0.46 vs best LLM-only 0.41; Llama 0.45 vs 0.28 LLM-only. On ARN near, CoT beat YARN (0.79 vs 0.69). A graph-edit-distance variant reached about 0.6 on MCQ but did worse on ARN.
limits: Small open models; mixed across benchmarks; mapping used embedding similarity that captures surface meaning.
agent_relevance: Mapping needs the right abstraction level, and the abstraction is the hard part. The code scorer alone is not enough.

source: Weitekamp & MacLellan (2026) SMTB: fast structure-mapping with tight bounds
finding: A mapping algorithm that maximises relational connectivity without privileging higher-order relations is faster and finds better mappings than SME v4 on large domains.
numbers: 515x faster than SME; about 50% better mappings in large nested domains. On 5,845 SME-corpus pairs: small (<64 entities) about equal (up to 1.05x); medium (65-128) 1.31x; large (>128) 1.80x on the SMTB objective and 1.52x on the SME objective. Structure mapping is NP-hard (quadratic-assignment-like).
limits: Authors evaluate largely on their own objective. Self-reported by the system's builders.
agent_relevance: Higher-order bias is not always needed; plain connectivity worked as well. A cheap connectivity score is enough for O7.

source: Weitekamp & MacLellan (2026): when higher-order bias fails
finding: Argues SME's higher-order bias can be an arbitrary effect of notation and can discard correct local matches.
numbers: Example: algebra equations where SME drops all other correspondences when one higher-order kernel fails, so it cannot see that only the right-hand side differs. Flat first-order representations are common in practice.
limits: Argument and worked examples, not human data.
agent_relevance: Do not require higher-order relations; score connected relational overlap on the representation the agent actually writes.

source: Forbus, Ferguson, Lovett & Gentner (2017) Extending SME to handle large-scale cognitive modeling (Cognitive Science 41)
finding: Review of 30 years of SME as a process model. The basic algorithm held up; greedy merge makes it polynomial time; the old separate rule sets for analogy, literal similarity and surface match were replaced by one overall similarity scheme.
numbers: Greedy merge builds up to 3 near-optimal global mappings in polynomial time. Visual oddity task: model solved 39 of 45 problems; the unsolved ones were hardest for people. Also used on AP physics and thermodynamics problem solving through analogy.
limits: Authors review their own programme. They admit no consensus on how central systematicity or pragmatics are, and that some models do not use systematicity.
agent_relevance: SME's search is cheap enough to run as a code step; use it as a scoring function, not as a claim of how people reason.

source: Forbus et al. (2017): evidence cited for systematicity and processing time course
finding: Review lists support for SME's local-to-global process: under a 600 ms deadline people showed no direction preference for metaphors; by 1,200 ms they did.
numbers: Wolff & Gentner (2011): 'Some suburbs are parasites' preferred over the reversed order in untimed tasks; no directional preference at 600 ms; forward advantage by 1,200 ms. Systematicity also steers inference direction (Bowdle & Gentner 1997).
limits: Secondary citation; underlying studies not opened.
agent_relevance: The fast first pass is symmetric; direction comes later. Do not expect direction-sensitive mapping from a fast pass.

source: Forbus et al. (2017): rival models and what is agreed
finding: Rival models (IAM, ACME, COPYCAT, TABLETOP, LISA) differ on whether systematicity is enforced. Wide agreement exists on structural consistency (one-to-one, parallel connectivity), not on how central pragmatics is.
numbers: Cited alternatives: Holyoak 1985 (pragmatics); Hummel & Holyoak 1997 (LISA); Krawczyk et al. 2004, 2005 (neural evidence for consistency).
limits: Rival-theory experiments were not opened; only the authors' summary.
agent_relevance: Keep the one-to-one rule hard and treat higher-order weighting as a tunable score (consistent with the SMTB result).

source: Alfieri, Nokes-Malach & Schunn (2013) Learning through case comparisons: a meta-analytic review (Educational Psychologist 48); 2011 conference abstract version
finding: Learning from comparing two cases beats other instruction, with real heterogeneity. The text opened is the 2011 SREE abstract, not the published paper.
numbers: 57 experiments, 336 tests. Random-effects d=.60 (95% CI .47 to .72) in the 2011 abstract. Q(56)=136.74, p<.001, I2=59%. Fail-safe N: 2,795 (experiments) and 5,244 (tests). A search summary of the published 2013 paper gives about d=.50.
limits: Abstract and published figures differ (.60 vs about .50). Published moderator findings were not opened.
agent_relevance: Comparing two cases is a medium-sized help in people. Cite about d=.5, not more.

source: Alfieri et al. (2013) moderators (search summary only)
finding: Search summary only: 4 of 15 moderators reliably mattered (objective of comparison, presenting a principle, content, lag to test). Finding only similarities beat similarities plus differences; giving the principle after the comparison helped.
numbers: Search snippet: 336 tests from 57 experiments, medium overall effect.
limits: Not opened (download of the PDF failed). Unverified.
agent_relevance: Check against the paper before using the moderator directions.

source: Loewenstein, Thompson & Gentner (1999) Analogical encoding facilitates knowledge transfer in negotiation (Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 6)
finding: Comparing two training cases made people far more likely to transfer the strategy to a new negotiation. Studying the same two cases separately transferred little.
numbers: Exp 1: transfer 50% with analogy training vs 19% baseline; compromises (suboptimal) fell. Exp 2 (management graduate students, dyads): contingency contract in 48% (13/27) of compare dyads vs 16% (5/31) of no-compare dyads; 'nearly three times' more likely. Exp 2 advantage about $64,000 (6%), t(56)=4.37, p<.001.
limits: Dyads, one domain (negotiation). Labeling the principle added nothing in Exp 2.
agent_relevance: Human evidence that aligning two cases lifts transfer. In the agent, two worked cases plus an explicit alignment may beat one case.

source: Loewenstein et al. (1999): background on unaided transfer (Gick & Holyoak; Gentner et al. 1993)
finding: Unaided transfer is rare and retrieval follows surface features, not structure.
numbers: Radiation problem solved by about 10% unaided; about 85% after an analogous story plus a hint (Gick & Holyoak). Gentner et al. 1993: stories recalled 55% of the time on surface match vs 12% on purely analogical match.
limits: Secondary citation inside a 1999 paper; originals not opened.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of a far analogue will fail on surface cues. Hand the agent the analogue, or retrieve by structure with code.

source: Gentner & Markman (1997) Structure mapping in analogy and similarity (American Psychologist 52)
finding: Review of the human evidence. Transfer is easier when corresponding objects look alike (transparency); a causal model lets people transfer even when objects do not look alike.
numbers: Gentner & Schumacher ship-panel study: faster learning of a second device with physical resemblance between corresponding parts, and with a causal explanation. Children show transparency effects early and systematicity effects later (Gentner & Toupin 1986). Authors suspect systematic explanation needs some domain knowledge.
limits: Narrative review by the theory's proposers.
agent_relevance: Expertise is a moderator: novices use surface looks. Do not assume the model, any more than a novice, can use deep structure unaided.

source: Donvito & Lieto (2026) Structural ranking of the cognitive plausibility of computational models of analogy and metaphor
finding: Ranks SME, CogSketch, METCL and LLMs on cognitive plausibility with the Minimal Cognitive Grid.
numbers: No headline numbers read beyond the abstract: three dimensions (functional/structural ratio, generality, performance match).
limits: Abstract and introduction only.
agent_relevance: Plausibility is not accuracy; only accuracy matters for the agent.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024, ICLR) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Telling an LLM to recall relevant past problems before solving beat zero-shot chain-of-thought on several tasks. This is analogy by recall, not structure mapping.
numbers: Codeforces, GPT-3.5-turbo-16k, Acc@1: 0-shot 8%, 0-shot CoT 9%, 3-shot CoT 11%, self-generated exemplars 13%, plus self-generated knowledge 15%. With text-davinci models, labelled few-shot CoT beat self-generation at small scales; self-generation overtook it at davinci-002 and -003. Best K=3 to 5 exemplars; K=1 hurt.
limits: Absolute gains small on Codeforces; extra output tokens; no mapping or constraint check; main math table garbled in extraction so GSM8K figures are not recorded.
agent_relevance: Cheap analogue recall helps only if the model is strong enough to write good analogues. At weak scale, hand-picked analogues are better.

source: Probing study (2025) The curious case of analogies: investigating analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Hidden-state probing of proportional and story analogies. Relational information is present in mid-upper layers when the answer is right; failures often show a missing relation, or failure to apply it to new entities.
numbers: No accuracy table recorded. Qualitative: success shows strong structural alignment between the situations; patching hidden states at key tokens helps 'to a certain extent'.
limits: Abstract and probing section only; no table copied.
agent_relevance: Failing to apply a known relation to new entities is the hole. A code-checked role mapping patches it.

source: Xu, Yan & Zhang (2026, ICML) Feature resemblance: theory of analogical reasoning in transformers
finding: Theory: entities with shared properties become aligned in representation space, which lets properties transfer; learning similarity before attributes matters.
numbers: Proofs in a minimal transformer; experiments up to 8B parameters agree only qualitatively.
limits: Stylised theory; does not test higher-order structure mapping.
agent_relevance: Analogy skill depends on training order, not prompt scaffold. Not a lever for our agent.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024): human variance and baseline differences
finding: Human letter-string accuracy changed between studies, and the GPT baselines differed from the earlier paper on several problem types.
numbers: Webb sample 57 students vs 46 per cell here; baseline differences on Predecessor and Fix Alphabet (GPT-3), Remove Redundant, Fix Alphabet, Sort (GPT-3.5), Remove Redundant and Sort (GPT-4).
limits: Replication of the GPT part is approximate (different model snapshots and prompts).
agent_relevance: Analogy scores are protocol dependent; compare arms inside one run.
